# The Department of Unfinished Things

On the morning the city decided to abolish the Department of Unfinished Things, Mara was repairing the spine of a cookbook whose author had stopped at soup.

There were eleven soups. The twelfth recipe consisted of the words *First, forgive your brother*, followed by a greasy thumbprint. Mara had spent several weeks determining whether this was an instruction or a dedication. In either case, the binding needed glue.

The abolition notice arrived in a yellow envelope.

“Is that bad?” asked the courier.

“It’s official,” Mara said. “There’s some overlap.”

He waited while she signed his receipt, then glanced around the office. Along one wall stood cabinets labeled with years. Along another stood cabinets labeled with reasons. The largest was marked SOMETHING CAME UP.

“What do you actually do here?”

“Mostly,” Mara said, “we keep things from getting into the water.”

***

The department occupied three rooms beneath the municipal swimming pool. On summer afternoons, sunlight came through the high windows in trembling blue rectangles. Above Mara’s desk, swimmers crossed the ceiling with the slow, distorted grace of furniture being moved upstairs.

Nobody remembered why unfinished things collected beneath a pool. The city’s founding charter referred only to “an appropriate low place.”

Things arrived by various means.

A half-knitted cardigan might appear in a drain basket. The opening chapters of a novel would collect behind a radiator. Once, a marriage proposal emerged from a drinking fountain, still warm and carrying the faint taste of pennies.

Mara catalogued them, stabilized them, and waited.

Sometimes their owners came back.

More often, they didn’t.

***

The notice gave her thirty days to empty the premises.

The department’s functions, it explained, would be absorbed by the Office of Records and Recreational Services. Its collection would be reviewed for retention, digitization, or appropriate disposal.

Mara read the sentence twice.

Then she opened the cabinet labeled GOOD INTENTIONS.

Inside, seventeen thousand promises shifted in their sleep.

She closed it gently.

At eleven, she telephoned the deputy administrator whose signature appeared on the notice.

“Disposal isn’t straightforward,” she explained.

“We have a contractor.”

“What kind?”

“A licensed one.”

“Licensed for what?”

There was a pause.

“Municipal materials.”

Mara looked at the drawer containing the bridge that had never reached the far bank.

“I see,” she said.

***

She had inherited the job from her father, who had inherited it from a woman everyone called Aunt Nell, including the mayor, though she was related to none of them.

Her father had taught Mara the filing system during school holidays.

“Never put an unfinished apology beside an unfinished accusation,” he told her. “They’ll keep each other going all night.”

“What about poems?”

“Flat drawers. Away from heat.”

“And inventions?”

“Depends what they eat.”

He had been an ordinary-looking man with thick fingers and a permanently loose button on his coat. He knew which abandoned ambitions could be safely folded and which needed room to stand.

He died before teaching her everything.

For eighteen years, she had been discovering the omissions.

***

That afternoon, a boy came in carrying a wooden bird.

He was perhaps twelve. The bird had one carved wing and one square block where a wing ought to be. Its eye was a pencil dot.

“My grandfather said you might take this.”

“Is he finished with it?”

“No. He died.”

“I’m sorry.”

The boy put the bird on the desk but kept a hand on its back.

“He was teaching me. We were going to make six.”

“What’s your name?”

“Eli.”

“Do you want to finish this one, Eli?”

He shook his head, then nodded, then looked annoyed with himself.

Mara brought him a chair.

“That’s a common category,” she said.

***

They sat for a while without talking.

Overhead, someone entered the pool badly. A flat slap traveled through the ceiling.

“Belly flop,” Eli said.

“Probably.”

“He said the trick was to take away everything that wasn’t a bird.”

“Your grandfather?”

“Yes.”

“That sounds difficult.”

“It was mostly shavings.”

Mara turned the wooden bird carefully. The completed wing was elegant, but the body still bore rough cuts. A shallow groove marked the place where the carver’s tool had slipped.

“May I keep it here for a week?” she asked.

“What happens after a week?”

“You can decide again.”

Eli considered this.

“Can I come see it?”

“Of course.”

He left the bird facing the window.

***

The trouble began four days later, when the contractors removed the cabinet labeled WHEN THERE’S TIME.

Mara had gone upstairs to argue about the electricity bill. By the time she returned, the cabinet was on a trolley and one of its doors had swung open.

A small holiday fell out.

It spread across the floor: a rented cottage, a railway platform, a strip of pale beach. Salt water touched the contractor’s boots.

He stared at it.

“That wasn’t in the assessment.”

“No,” Mara said. “It wouldn’t be.”

By evening, three streets smelled of the sea. People stopped working to look west. A dentist walked out during a routine cleaning and bought a straw hat.

The cabinet took nine hours to repack.

***

The deputy administrator visited the following morning.

His name was Venn. He wore a gray suit and carried a notebook so new its covers resisted opening.

“I understand there’s been a leak.”

“Several.”

“Can we contain them?”

“We were containing them.”

He looked around, perhaps noticing for the first time that the office was less a neglected storeroom than a place under constant, delicate pressure.

From a drawer came the sound of someone practicing four bars of violin.

“That one started in 1936,” Mara said. “She nearly came back for it in 1982.”

“What happened?”

“She heard herself and remembered being bad at it.”

Venn wrote something down.

“Does anything here ever simply end?”

“Yes,” Mara said. “But not through disposal.”

***

To demonstrate, she took him into the smallest room.

It contained a table, two chairs, and a stove disconnected from any chimney.

On a shelf sat a ceramic bowl repaired with ordinary glue. Inside lay a collection of tiny objects: a blue ticket, a shoelace, a brass screw, a leaf that had dried almost white.

“These are finished,” Mara said.

“Then why keep them?”

“They’re the labels. We keep the labels.”

She picked up the ticket.

“A woman planned to become a dancer. Practiced for nine years. One day she realized she preferred repairing bicycles.”

“So she failed.”

“No. She opened a bicycle shop.”

“What happened to the dancing?”

“Nothing happened to it. That was the point.”

***

Venn looked at the cold stove.

“And that?”

“For things people choose to stop.”

“You burn them?”

“Not exactly.”

“Then exactly what?”

Mara hesitated. Her father would have answered better. He could explain impossible procedures in the patient tone other people used for changing a fuse.

“The stove takes the waiting out,” she said.

“Could we put everything through it?”

“Not unless the owners choose.”

“Many must be dead.”

“Yes.”

“Or impossible to locate.”

“Yes.”

He closed his notebook.

“You understand my problem.”

“I do,” Mara said. “There’s a swimming pool upstairs and a budget deficit, and no convenient column for this.”

For the first time, he almost smiled.

***

That night, Mara stayed late to examine the old manuals.

Most concerned humidity, shelving, and the handling of abandoned theatrical productions, which were liable to expand when admired.

At the back of a maintenance ledger, she found an entry in Aunt Nell’s handwriting.

*During the winter closure, held public evenings. Tea essential. Do not permit speeches.*

Below that, in her father’s writing:

*People will claim what is not theirs if it looks impressive. Verify carefully.*

And below that:

*Some things belong to more than one person.*

Mara read until the lights upstairs went out.

Then she opened her own bottom drawer.

Inside was a letter she had begun to her father three weeks before he died.

***

It was not a dramatic letter.

She had meant to tell him that she did not want the department.

She wanted a job above ground, perhaps in a botanical garden. She wanted to work with things whose growth could be measured. She wanted Saturdays untroubled by someone else’s abandoned opera.

The letter began, *I know how much this means to you.*

She had never found a second sentence she could bear to write.

After his funeral, she put the letter in the drawer. Then she stayed for a month to organize the collection.

The month became a season.

There were always items requiring immediate attention.

She shut the drawer and went to buy tea.

***

The first public evening drew six people, not counting Venn, who said he was attending only to observe.

Mara placed a notice outside:

**HAVE YOU LEFT SOMETHING UNFINISHED?  
THURSDAY, SIX TO EIGHT.  
NO OBLIGATION TO RESUME.**

A retired baker reclaimed a plan to learn Italian.

A woman brought in a box of wedding favors from a marriage that had never happened. She had already removed the sugared almonds.

Two brothers arrived separately to ask about the same boat.

When Mara brought it out, they stood on opposite sides of the table.

“You made the keel too deep,” one said.

“You bought the wrong plans,” said the other.

“Tea?” Mara asked.

***

By the third Thursday, the queue reached the pool entrance.

Some people came only to look. Others arrived convinced they had forgotten something important and grew irritated when Mara could not tell them what.

A man claimed an unfinished symphony until it began playing. He admitted he had hoped it would already be nearly done.

A woman retrieved a degree she had abandoned twenty-seven years earlier.

“I’m not enrolling anywhere,” she said quickly.

“You don’t have to.”

“I only want to see what I knew.”

She sat in the corner reading until closing.

Venn washed cups. He had taken off his jacket. Nobody asked him whether this was an efficient use of municipal resources.

***

Eli came every week.

At first he only visited the bird. Then he asked whether he could sand it.

Mara found sandpaper in a cabinet labeled PREPARATIONS, where nearly anything useful could be found if one was willing to move enough equipment for camping trips.

He worked beside the window.

He did not carve the second wing.

Instead, he smoothed the square block until it was pleasant to hold.

“Would that bother him?” Eli asked one evening.

“Your grandfather?”

“He wanted it to look real.”

“I didn’t know him.”

“Everyone else says he’d love it.”

“They may be right.”

“But you don’t know.”

“No.”

Eli seemed relieved by this.

***

Not everything improved.

Someone reclaimed an argument and immediately continued it in the corridor.

An unfinished political manifesto escaped into the ventilation system. For two days, every announcement at the swimming pool began with a statement of principles.

A woman found the dress she had planned to wear after losing weight. She stared at it for a long time.

“Can you make it bigger?”

“I can give you the number of a seamstress.”

“I used to be good at sewing.”

She touched the fabric.

“Actually, may I borrow your scissors?”

Mara found a pair. The woman sat down and began unpicking the narrow sleeves, placing each thread neatly beside her.

***

On the twenty-sixth day, Venn brought the revised decision.

The department would still close.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

Mara set down the inventory.

“Despite all this?”

“The building needs structural repairs. The pool’s losing water into the foundation. Your rooms have to be emptied either way.”

It was such a practical problem that for a moment she could think of nothing to say.

“Why didn’t the notice mention that?”

“Different department.”

Above them, a child ran along the poolside. A whistle sounded.

Venn placed a second document on her desk.

“There is, however, provision for relocating certain public-facing services.”

“How much provision?”

“Not enough for the cabinets.”

They looked toward SOMETHING CAME UP.

***

The answer came from the brothers with the boat.

They had spent three weeks arguing about it before discovering that neither wanted to build it anymore.

One wanted to fish. The other got seasick.

They put the boat through the stove, where it made a sound like a wave reaching pebbles. What remained was a small washer.

Afterward, over tea, Mara mentioned the problem of storage.

“Why keep it all together?” the seasick brother asked.

“It’s always been together.”

“So were our tools. That’s why we never found anything.”

His brother nodded toward the crowded office.

“There are empty rooms all over this city.”

“Yes,” Mara said.

“Use those.”

***

The collection moved slowly.

The library accepted unfinished books, with safeguards against their mingling with the finished ones.

The music school took compositions, except for three unstable operas, which went to the old fire station.

The bicycle repair shop accepted inventions of modest appetite.

Apologies remained difficult. Mara found homes for some at the mediation center, but others required individual arrangements. One had to be kept beside a telephone that would never ring.

Volunteers learned the labels.

They made mistakes.

A box of unattempted recipes briefly filled a church kitchen with invisible onions.

Still, each evening, the department grew emptier.

For the first time, Mara could hear the actual plumbing.

***

On the last afternoon, Eli came to collect his bird.

He had painted the finished wing brown and the unfinished block blue.

“Is it done?” Mara asked.

“I think so.”

He turned it in his hands.

“It’s not what we were making.”

“No.”

“But I like holding this part.”

His thumb rested on the smooth blue wood.

Mara wrapped it in a towel, which he immediately removed.

“I’ll carry it.”

After he left, she stood in the empty office. The cabinets were gone. Pale rectangles marked the walls.

She opened her bottom drawer.

The letter lay exactly where she had left it.

She took it to the smallest room.

***

Venn found her sitting beside the stove.

“Everything accounted for?”

“Almost.”

He noticed the paper.

“Do you need me to go?”

“No. I don’t think so.”

She read the first sentence once more.

Then she took out a pen.

For a long time, she listened to the water moving overhead.

Finally she wrote:

*I didn’t want this job. I did it anyway. Some of it has been good.*

She considered adding more. An explanation. An apology. A list of things she had postponed.

Instead, she signed her name.

“Will you keep it?” Venn asked.

Mara folded the letter.

“Yes,” she said, surprised. “I believe I will.”

***

The new office was a desk inside the central library.

Mara worked there three days a week. On the other two, she trained at the botanical garden, learning the names of plants she had previously known only by sight.

The work was less simple than she had imagined.

Some seeds waited years. Some branches had to be cut away. A tree could appear healthy while quietly dying at its center.

She liked it anyway.

At the library, people still came with boxes, notebooks, promises, and plans.

Mara offered them a chair.

Outside her office, the old notice hung beneath a smaller, newer sign:

**YOU MAY ALSO TAKE IT HOME.**
